VideoBlocks Group Buy: A Practical Guide to Finding and Editing Stock Footage

Stock footage can save a production day when a video needs a shot the crew cannot easily capture. It can establish a place, bridge an interview edit, or show an action the narration describes. A successful search begins with the edit. Decide what the audience needs to see and when they need to see it. Then examine possible clips for their framing, motion, technical quality, and suitability for the project. A visually attractive clip earns its place when it helps tell the story.

SEOGBTools lists VideoBlocks as a stock footage product. If someone describes the offer as Storyblocks access, confirm the exact library, subscription type, and applicable license. The provider's listing and the stock library's license answer different questions. Use the listing to ask what access is supplied and the current agreement to determine whether the person or company making the production can use the material as planned. Check those details before committing an edit or promising delivery.

Write the missing shot into the script

Imagine an editor assembling a ninety-second interview for a neighborhood bicycle shop. The owner describes how customers arrive with an unfamiliar sound, show where it comes from, and watch a mechanic examine the bike. The editor has a good interview and a few shots of the shop. The footage is missing a simple close-up that explains the difference between a spinning wheel and a hand testing the brake lever. An overhead view of a city bike lane might look impressive, but it cannot show that movement.

Go through the script and underline every sentence that refers to a visible action. Mark which actions the footage already shows. Read the remaining lines aloud and decide whether an audience member can understand them with the current pictures. Sometimes a brief moment of the interview's existing footage does the job. When a new shot is needed, describe it in terms of what must be visible. An effective note might say “close-up of a hand squeezing a bicycle brake lever, room for a title at left.”

Prioritize shots by purpose. An essential shot demonstrates something the narration cannot describe efficiently. A supporting shot establishes context, lets a transition breathe, or makes a cut less abrupt. Record the placeholder position and how much time you have for the action. A seven-second interval may require one action and a pause at its end. Ask whether the shot can be constructed from an existing take, recorded quickly with the client, or sourced as stock. Local footage is often the right answer for a scene viewers could mistake for the client’s property.

Build a brief for footage search

Record the sequence format before browsing. Include orientation, delivery resolution, approximate length, and where captions or logos will sit. A vertical ad could need the hand near the center, with enough space above it for captions. A wide website video might need an empty left side for text. When both formats matter, describe both compositions in the brief and look for enough room to create the alternate version without cropping out the action.

Add the physical features that affect continuity. A bicycle mechanic in an indoor workshop might be lit from one side, with a warm background and a neutral work surface. A rainy outdoor clip has a different role. Lighting and camera angle matter as much as the subject. Include a reference frame from your own production when sharing the brief with other editors. A still from the approved scene gives them a more concrete target than a sentence such as “find something cinematic.”

Distinguish requirements from choices that can change. If your next shot follows a hand from left to right, screen direction may be a requirement. The exact color of an anonymous jacket could be flexible unless its owner appears in the following shot. If the clip is intended to illustrate an example instead of portraying the actual client, maintain enough distance between the stock scene and the client's identity. Use authentic client footage for landmarks, staff, and products when the audience expects to see those people or places.

Search with nouns, actions, and camera language

Start with one phrase the subject can be described by. For the bicycle project, “mechanic checks bike brake” is a reasonable first search. If you only see finished bicycles parked in shops, add the action “squeezing brake lever.” If the results miss the type of bicycle, try “road bike brake lever close-up.” Change one part of the phrase at a time so you can tell what improved relevance. Use the library’s supported filters for properties such as orientation and resolution when available.

Search for how the footage should move. “Locked camera” can help you find a frame that holds steady behind text. “Tracking shot” may keep pace with a moving subject. If you need slow motion, review the listed frame rate and the visual motion itself. An existing slow-motion clip may have a baked-in speed and behave differently when you retime it. Preview the full selection so you know when the usable movement begins, whether it repeats, and whether there is enough footage around your cut point.

Build a shortlist with two reasonable candidates and one fallback. Record the asset title, identifier, library link, duration, and why the shot works. A fallback can be an owned still, a tighter crop of a longer interview shot, or a clip you have already cleared. Mark any shot you liked but could not verify for the project. Keep previews labeled as previews in the editing bin and replace them deliberately with the corresponding downloaded media after checking access.

Judge the clip in the edit

A thumbnail cannot tell you how a clip begins or ends. Play from the first frame and look for camera settlement, focus changes, and the exact moment the action completes. If the narration names an action at second twelve, place the movement so viewers have already oriented themselves when the word is spoken. Watch the cut at normal speed. A split second of activity often reads differently when seen on a busy phone display than when inspected one frame at a time on a large monitor.

Check the clip beside footage already in the sequence. Moving from a warm workshop to a cool office can make the viewer think the scene changed. A new camera height may be fine in an establishing shot and distracting in a close sequence of actions. Compare shadow direction, apparent time of day, and the direction the main subject leaves a frame. Adjust only what the shot can tolerate. Correcting mild differences in tone may be easy. Convincing the audience that two visibly different workspaces are the same room is a separate problem.

Use the part of the clip that helps the story. If the point is to show a press on a brake lever, trim away the part where the hand has not entered. Keep enough time to establish whose hand it is and what it is touching. A faster cut might make the sequence feel lively but obscure the physical demonstration. The best edit balances clarity with pace and gives titles and captions enough time to be read.

Assemble B-roll around the spoken explanation

Use the interview as the reference track. First, arrange the speaker's sentences so they tell one understandable story. Next, mark places where a visual explains what was said, covers an edit, or changes the level of detail. Most supporting shots should have a clear job. An establishing shot can set the environment. A medium shot can introduce a process. A close-up can show the position of the brake lever. Try that order, then remove any frame that duplicates what the clip before it already explained.

When a sentence changes topic, the visual transition can acknowledge the move. Suppose the owner goes from describing a brake noise to explaining the booking process. Hold the workshop visual through the last brake sentence. Then cut back to the speaker or an authentic booking visual as the next point starts. An unrelated stock image of someone filling a form can be confusing if it resembles a different business. Try letting the original speaker remain on screen while the audience hears the useful detail.

Test crops for all delivery versions. A wide source may frame the mechanic and bicycle comfortably at full width but lose the repair when cropped vertically. Move the crop to the key object and check the position throughout the shot. Preview the video with captions on, since captions can overlap the action. If two characters or objects need to remain visible and their spacing prevents a good vertical crop, choose another take or use a layout that preserves what the explanation needs.

Confirm technical compatibility before the final export

Check source dimensions, frame rate, runtime, and codec against the sequence. A higher resolution source gives you more cropping room but can require proxies for responsive editing. A different frame rate can be workable, depending on motion and delivery needs, so test the exact clip instead of relying on a spec title. Inspect the result on playback. Look at spokes, patterned surfaces, and fast hand movement where differences in cadence become apparent.

Check the beginning and end of each replacement file after relinking. Some previews contain a different lead-in or outro. Ensure the action still matches the words and the frames around it are free from unintended marks or transitions. If an original stock clip carries audio you do not need, mute it before balancing the interview. If it carries useful ambient sound, review whether that sound belongs with the rest of the scene and is covered by the same intended use.

Keep a small delivery checklist. Scrub through any end frames where a stock clip ends near the next section. Review captions at phone size. Play the deliverable on a device other than the editing computer. Check for a watermark, offline media, or a still frame where footage should move. Save the master separately from versions for different platforms. A render log with aspect ratio, date, and project version helps you identify exactly what the client approved.

Review the applicable license and download records

Confirm the exact library and agreement that govern your download. Storyblocks publishes information about different license arrangements and what they cover. If the access you are considering is presented under the VideoBlocks name, ask which service actually provides the files and which legal entity supplies the entitlement. For a client production, identify whether you are the person, team, or organization that needs to be covered and which party will publish the final video.

List intended uses before checking the agreement. Write down the channels, whether the content is paid advertising, who receives the final edit, and whether any separate project files are being delivered. A request for the original source clip deserves its own check. Storyblocks explains that handing an unedited original stock file to a client is not permitted under the scenario described in its client-project help article. Review the relevant agreement and seek clarification for your own delivery rather than assuming permission for every handoff.

Check the terms for future edits, reuses, or publications when the subscription ends. Different plans and projects can come with different conditions, so record the rule that applies to your intended work. If the rights remain unclear, replace the shot with an asset whose terms you can verify or use footage you own. A replacement made during the rough cut costs less than a replacement after a campaign has been delivered to several channels.

Build a file system the next editor can understand

Give each stock clip a stable folder and record the library identifier next to its editorial label. The filename may tell you little about why the file was chosen. A short entry such as “brake lever close-up, shot used under explanation of pad movement” is enough to find its place. Save the asset reference, the applicable terms, and any purchase or download records you are allowed to retain. Keep previews and cleared files apart in your production library to prevent an accidental substitution.

When handing over a project, outline which footage can be included in the delivery and which requires the receiving party to obtain their own authorized access. A project file can still contain placeholders and a list of asset IDs when you cannot send the originals. Check the client’s expectations before final delivery. The person producing the edit, purchasing the license, and receiving the final render may each assume the others have handled the stock rights.

Use a simple audit at the end of the edit. Verify that every stock shot shown in the final cut appears in the production log. Review any shots added during late changes and confirm that the applicable record is present. Attach the reference list to the project folder. If someone changes the final aspect ratio or creates a new edit later, the original asset notes will tell them what was used and which terms they need to check again.

Run a small test before buying access for a deadline

Start with one genuinely missing shot from an existing timeline. Search for three candidates, try one preview in the cut where permitted, and check whether the result improves the sequence. Time the search and review. If it takes longer to explain why the stock shot does not quite work than it would take to record a clean insert, a simple local shoot may be the better choice. If the clip depicts a location or condition the crew cannot access, stock can be an efficient solution.

Ask the seller to describe the particular workspace, what is included, the term of access, and how to get help with the relevant license. If your deliverable depends on a specific resolution, plan, asset category, or client use case, ask about that exact requirement. The point of the pilot is to learn whether the service fits a repeatable production task with terms you can document.

Handle stock footage when the client wants a recognizable location

A local business might ask for an opening shot that makes the audience immediately recognize its town. Treat that as a separate requirement from showing a generic urban setting. If geography is essential, compare identifying features in the clip with a reliable map or with photographs the client owns. Read the asset description carefully and check signs, landmarks, and visible transit markings in the full preview. When the stock clip cannot be identified confidently, ask the client for a short filmed exterior or use another visual that does not make a geographical claim.

The same principle applies to a shot that could pass as the client's staff, premises, or product. Decide whether the shot illustrates a general concept or purports to show the real organization. Read the caption, narration, and surrounding shots together. A title naming a business followed immediately by a stock exterior might imply that the exterior belongs to it. Put more explicit context in the sequence or use the footage as a clearly illustrative insert where viewers can understand its purpose.

Make a fallback version before the client review

Build a short alternate sequence for any high-priority shot whose clearance or fit is still uncertain. Use a clip the client owns or an original graphic that explains the same point. Keep the alternate under the same narration and compare the running times. If the stock shot is unavailable, you can switch versions while keeping the edit coherent. This is especially useful for a sequence with captions timed to the action.

Tell the reviewer which shot is provisional, why it is provisional, and when you need a decision. Ask for feedback about what the picture communicates. A comment such as “this looks good” can mean the color works while the audience still misses the important action. Give the reviewer a concrete question, such as whether they can tell which component is being tested. Keep the approval and final asset details with your edit notes. When a future cut uses the same sequence, the editor can see why that shot was chosen and which replacement was considered.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use stock footage in a client video?

Check the specific license, who it covers, and the planned distribution. Storyblocks provides separate guidance for client projects and explains the limits on handing over original files. Keep the applicable agreement and download record with the project.

Is a video preview enough for delivery?

Use previews to assess an edit when that use is permitted. Replace temporary files with the corresponding authorized downloads, then check the finished render for watermarking and technical issues. Keep the preview names distinct in your editing bin.

Do I need 4K footage for every project?

Choose the version that fits the sequence and the amount of reframing you need. Higher resolution may give you room to crop, particularly when a horizontal source needs a vertical version. It does not solve a clip whose subject moves out of frame or whose composition conflicts with your captions.

What makes a useful shortlist?

Include only clips that can do the job identified in the script. Save the identifiers, preview links, technical properties, and reasons for choosing each one. A good fallback works if your preferred clip fails the quality or licensing check.

How many stock shots should I use?

Work from the story. A clear demonstration may need only one or two inserts. Another project may need several short context shots. Test whether each clip gives the audience information they need, bridges a justified cut, or supports timing without confusing the setting.
